result: FOXC1 is induced by laminar shear stress (LSS) but not by oscillatory shear stress (OSS) in cultured lymphatic endothelial cells, while FOXC2 is induced by both LSS and OSS. This differential regulation was demonstrated through in vitro flow experiments showing FOXC1 expression increased under LSS but was slightly reduced under OSS compared to static conditions.
evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C106, C107, C174, and C175 are directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3, which demonstrates differential FOXC1 and FOXC2 expression under different flow conditions. The quantification in Figure 3b shows statistically significant differences in nuclear intensity between conditions, providing robust evidence for this differential regulation.

result: Inducible, endothelial-specific deletion of Foxc1 postnatally impaired lymphatic valve maturation in mice without significantly affecting total valve number. The proportion of mature, v-shaped or semilunar bi-leaflet valve structures was significantly reduced in EC-Foxc1-KO mice at P6-P7, a phenotype observed with both Cdh5-CreERT2 and Prox1-CreERT2 strains.
evaluation: Claims C4, C54, C55, C58, C60, and C61 are well-supported by quantitative data in Figure 2u,v and Figure 2—figure supplement 2e,f showing no significant change in total valve number but significant reduction in mature valve proportion. The use of multiple Cre strains (C55, C58, C60) strengthens the conclusion that FOXC1 function is maintained during postnatal valve maturation (C61).

result: Postnatal deletion of Foxc2 beginning at P1 induced lymphatic valve degeneration, significantly reducing both total valve number and the percentage of mature valves. Many valve regions showed collecting vessel constriction indicative of regression, and α9-integrin expression was reduced, indicating impaired valve maturation processes.
evaluation: Claims C5, C63, C64, C65, C66, C67, and C68 are strongly supported by quantitative data in Figure 2w,x and immunostaining data in Figure 2g-l. The observation of chylous effusion in 13% of mutants (C64) and reduced α9-integrin expression (C67) provide additional evidence for valve degeneration and impaired maturation.

result: Combined deletion of Foxc1 and Foxc2 resulted in a synergistic response with exacerbated valve degeneration compared to Foxc2 deletion alone. At P6, 61.5% of EC-Foxc1; Foxc2-DKO mice developed severe chylous ascites and chylothorax, PROX1-high valve regions were nearly absent, and lymphatic collecting vessel hierarchy was markedly abnormal with a primitive plexus-like appearance.
evaluation: Claims C6, C71, C72, C73, C74, C75, C76, C78, and C79 are well-supported by data in Figure 2m-p,q-t,y showing the severe phenotype in compound mutants. The quantitative data (C71: 48/78 mice with chylous ascites) and immunostaining showing near-complete absence of valves (C73) and primitive vascular architecture (C75) provide strong evidence for synergistic effects.

result: FOXC1 and FOXC2 colocalize within nuclei of intraluminal valve leaflets in adult mice, but with distinct spatial patterns: FOXC1 expression is most highly enriched at the leading free-edge of valve leaflets exposed to laminar pulsatile shear stress, while FOXC2 is more highly enriched in valve sinuses and surrounding lymphangion exposed to reciprocating shear stress.
evaluation: Claims C46, C47, C48, C172, and C173 are directly supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1 showing differential spatial distribution of FOXC1 and FOXC2 in mature valves. The correlation with flow patterns (C48, C172, C173) is supported by citations to prior work characterizing shear stress in these regions.

result: FOXC1 knockdown in human lymphatic endothelial cells increased focal adhesions and actin stress fibers, with substantial increase in transverse actin stress fiber formation associated with increased phosphorylation of MLC2, indicative of increased actomyosin contractility. This was potentiated under both oscillatory and laminar shear stress, and cells lost their ability to properly orient in the direction of LSS.
evaluation: Claims C7, C8, C114, C115, C116, C117, C118, and C119 are well-supported by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 4a,b. The immunostaining shows clear increases in stress fibers and p-MLC2 colocalization in FOXC1-KD cells, with quantitative evidence of impaired adhesion and viability.

result: FOXC2 knockdown in human lymphatic endothelial cells increased focal adherens junctions and disrupted cell junctions. FOXC2-KD LECs were characterized by modest p-MLC2 signal colocalized mostly to the cortical actin ring and discontinuous VE-Cadherin junctions, in contrast to the focal adhesions observed with FOXC1 knockdown.
evaluation: Claims C9, C10, C120, C125, C133, and C134 are supported by in vitro experimental data in Figure 4b,c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b showing distinct phenotypes between FOXC1-KD and FOXC2-KD cells. The differential localization of p-MLC2 and formation of adherens junctions vs focal adhesions provides clear evidence for separate roles.

result: FOXC1 knockdown mostly induced formation of vinculin-positive and paxillin-positive focal adhesions at the tip of actin stress fibers, while FOXC2 knockdown mostly induced formation of vinculin-positive and paxillin-positive adherens junctions associated with the cortical actin ring. Combined knockdown induced formation of both types, demonstrating that FOXC1 and FOXC2 have separate yet complementary roles in regulating LEC cytoskeletal organization.
evaluation: Claims C131, C132, C135, and C136 are well-supported by immunostaining data in Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b showing differential localization of focal adhesion markers. The observation that combined knockdown produces both phenotypes (C135) strongly supports the conclusion of separate but complementary roles (C136).

result: PRICKLE1, ARHGAP21, and ARHGAP23 are novel transcriptional targets of FOXC1 and FOXC2 in lymphatic endothelial cells. RNA-seq showed significant downregulation of these genes in LEC-Foxc1; Foxc2-DKO embryos, and ChIP assays demonstrated direct binding of FOXC1 and FOXC2 to evolutionarily conserved regions in the PRICKLE1 and ARHGAP21 loci, while FOXC2 showed specificity for the ARHGAP23 locus.
evaluation: Claims C142, C146-C153, and C158 are well-supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 5a and ChIP assay data in Figure 5e-j and Figure 5—figure supplement 1e-h. The combination of expression data and direct binding evidence provides strong support for these genes as transcriptional targets. The negative control ChIP experiment validates specificity.

result: Prickle1 expression is concentrated on the free edges of PROX1-high valve leaflets in vivo. Postnatal deletion of Foxc1 reduced Prickle1 expression within leaflet free-edge cells while other valve leaflet LECs retained modest expression, whereas deletion of Foxc2 or both Foxc1 and Foxc2 resulted in strong and broad reduction of Prickle1 throughout the lymphatic vasculature.
evaluation: Claims C154, C155, C156, and C157 are supported by immunostaining data in Figure 5k-p, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, and Videos 5-7 showing spatial distribution of Prickle1 and differential effects of Foxc1 vs Foxc2 deletion. The data clearly demonstrate the distinct patterns of Prickle1 reduction in different mutants.

result: Cytoskeletal and junctional changes induced by FOXC1 and FOXC2 inactivation are mediated by increased ROCK activation. ROCK inhibition with Y-27632 rescued cytoskeletal integrity changes induced by FOXC1 inactivation and junctional integrity changes induced by FOXC2 inactivation in vitro, demonstrating that key targets downstream of FOXC1 and FOXC2 function to negatively regulate RhoA/ROCK activation in LECs.
evaluation: Claims C11, C12, C13, C159, C161, and C162 are well-supported by in vitro rescue experiments shown in Figure 6a-d. The quantification of F-actin and p-MLC2 area demonstrates that ROCK inhibition reduces these parameters to control levels in both FOXC1-KD and FOXC2-KD cells, providing strong evidence for ROCK-mediated effects.

result: ROCK inhibition in vivo rescued junctional integrity changes induced by inactivation of FOXC2 and partially ameliorated valve degeneration in Foxc2 mutants, but did not rescue near-complete lymphatic valve degeneration in EC-Foxc1; Foxc2-DKO mutants. Foxc2 mutants administered Y-27632 retained significantly higher total valve number and increased proportion of mature valves compared to vehicle-treated mutants, though still lower than controls.
evaluation: Claims C14, C15, C163, C164, C165, C166, and C167 are supported by in vivo rescue experiments shown in Figure 7 and Figure 8. The quantitative data in Figure 7i,j,k show partial rescue in Foxc2 mutants but not in compound mutants, and Figure 8c,d,g,h demonstrates improved junction integrity in both mutant lines with ROCK inhibition.

result: FOXC2 can functionally substitute for FOXC1 during lymphatic valve development, maintenance, and maturation. Using Foxc1c2 knock-in mice where the Foxc2 coding region was recombined into the Foxc1 locus, total lymphatic valve number and valve maturation were not significantly changed in Foxc1c2/c2 mice compared to controls.
evaluation: Claims C169, C170, C171, and C186 are well-supported by data from the Foxc1c2 knock-in mouse experiments shown in Figure 9. The quantification in Figure 9o,p demonstrates no significant differences in valve number or maturation, and immunostaining confirms loss of FOXC1 with maintained FOXC2 expression in the Foxc1 locus.

result: LECs in wild-type mice are elongated, organized, aligned with flow direction, and have continuous cell-cell junctions. EC-specific inactivation of Foxc2 resulted in more rounded cells with disrupted junctions, while inactivation of both Foxc1 and Foxc2 severely impaired LEC organization with more spherical cells, poor elongation, and broader distribution of VE-Cadherin at junctions indicative of increased overlapping junctions, suggesting separate roles for FOXC1 and FOXC2 in regulating LEC intercellular junctions.
evaluation: Claims C88, C89, C90, C91, and C92 are supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4a-h and Videos 1-4. The distinct junction phenotypes in Foxc2 mutants (discontinuous) vs compound mutants (both discontinuous and overlapping) provide clear evidence for separate roles in junction regulation.

result: A significantly greater number of apoptotic cell bodies were detected throughout lymphatic collecting vessels of EC-Foxc1; Foxc2-DKO mice compared to littermate controls, with apoptotic bodies more frequently observed in closer proximity to branched regions potentially indicating areas of valve degeneration.
evaluation: Claims C95 and C96 are supported by quantification data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4i-k showing significantly increased apoptosis in compound mutants. The spatial distribution near branched regions (C96) is an observation from the data, though the interpretation as valve degeneration areas is inferential.

result: FOXC1 and FOXC2 have complementary roles in regulating lymphatic collecting vessel function. FOXC2 has a predominant role in maintaining LEC valve identity, while FOXC1 functions cooperatively with FOXC2 to refine valve maturation processes. Both transcription factors are required to maintain valve and LEC barrier integrity, with FOXC1 controlling focal adhesions and FOXC2 regulating adherens junctions.
evaluation: Claims C80, C81, C97, and C136 represent integrative conclusions drawn from multiple experimental results including in vivo phenotypes (Figure 2), in vitro knockdown experiments (Figure 4), and rescue experiments (Figures 6-8). The conclusions are well-supported by the collective evidence showing distinct but complementary functions.

result: FOXC1 and FOXC2 are mediators of mechanotransduction in the postnatal lymphatic vasculature. Mechanical stress induced by flow differentially regulates LEC FOXC1 and FOXC2 expression, and both transcription factors function to negatively regulate perturbed activation of Rho/ROCK signaling in LECs downstream of shear stress-sensing mechanisms. Response to differing mechanical stimuli is key for the induction of FOXC1 or FOXC2 expression to control their separate functions.
evaluation: Claims C16, C109, C168, and C189 represent major conclusions integrating multiple lines of evidence: differential regulation by shear stress (Figure 3), spatial expression patterns correlating with flow (Figure 1), functional roles in cytoskeletal organization (Figure 4), and ROCK-mediated effects (Figures 6-8). The evidence collectively supports these mechanotransduction roles.

result: No correlation was observed between FOXC1 and FOXC2 expression under different shear stress conditions in cultured LECs.
evaluation: Claim C108 is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-c demonstrating low R² values (0.119-0.199) for correlations between FOXC1 and FOXC2 nuclear intensity under static, OSS, and LSS conditions, indicating independent regulation.

result: Combined knockdown of FOXC1 and FOXC2 resulted in a similar phenotype to FOXC2-KD LECs in terms of p-MLC2 and F-actin distribution, suggesting a rate-limiting effect of FOXC1 in the control of actomyosin contractility.
evaluation: Claims C121 and C122 are supported by data in Figure 4b showing that combined knockdown does not produce a more severe phenotype than FOXC2-KD alone. However, the interpretation of a "rate-limiting effect" (C122) is somewhat speculative and could benefit from additional mechanistic investigation.

result: A greater distribution of overlapping VE-Cadherin-positive junctions was observed in FOXC1-KD LECs, while FOXC2-KD LECs showed discontinuous junctions. Combined FOXC1/FOXC2-KD LECs showed both overlapping and discontinuous junctions, indicating separate roles for FOXC1 and FOXC2 in regulation of intercellular junctions.
evaluation: Claims C124, C126, and C127 are supported by in vitro immunostaining data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a showing distinct junction phenotypes. This recapitulates the in vivo observations and strengthens the conclusion of separate roles in junction regulation.

result: The reduction of FOXC1 expression observed in collecting vessels of EC-Foxc2-KO mice in vivo is likely attributable to reduced flow as a result of perturbed barrier integrity and increased leakiness from lymphatic collecting vessels.
evaluation: Claim C110 is an inference based on the observation of reduced FOXC1 expression in Foxc2 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g) and known effects of Foxc2 deletion on barrier integrity. However, this mechanism was not directly tested (e.g., by measuring flow rates or testing whether restoring barrier function restores FOXC1 expression), making the causal link uncertain.

result: Cytoskeletal signaling, specifically RhoA/ROCK, is a potential therapeutic target in lymphatic pathologies and for treatment of hereditary forms of lymphedema.
evaluation: Claims C17 and C201 are speculative conclusions based on the observation that ROCK inhibition can ameliorate some phenotypes in mouse models (Figures 6-8). However, the partial rescue (only in Foxc2 mutants, not compound mutants) and lack of testing in human disease models or other lymphatic pathologies limits the strength of this therapeutic claim. This represents a reasonable hypothesis for future work rather than a demonstrated therapeutic approach.

result: The markedly abnormal branching pattern observed in EC-Foxc1; Foxc2-DKO mice is likely a result of accelerated valve regression and ectopic sprouting from these regions to compensate drainage from areas of perturbed flow.
evaluation: Claim C78 is an inference based on prior observations of ectopic sprouting in Foxc2 mutants (C77) and the phenotype in compound mutants. However, the mechanism was not directly tested (e.g., by lineage tracing or time-course analysis to demonstrate sprouting from degenerating valves), making this interpretation uncertain though plausible.

result: Although FOXC1 and FOXC2 have the same DNA-binding capacity, their transcriptional targets are likely to be different in cells under oscillatory shear stress or laminar shear stress.
evaluation: Claim C193 is a speculation based on observed differences in expression and function under different flow conditions. While the ChIP data (Figure 5) shows some differential binding (e.g., FOXC2 specificity for ARHGAP23), comprehensive transcriptional profiling under different flow conditions would be needed to definitively establish flow-dependent differences in target genes.

result: Background knowledge and prior work establishing the context for the current study, including: roles of FOXC2 and other transcription factors in lymphatic development and disease; lymphatic valve formation and function; FOXC1/FOXC2 family relationships; human disease associations; prior work on FOXC2 function; shear stress effects on LECs; RhoA/ROCK signaling; PCP pathway; mechanosensing proteins; and related mouse models.
evaluation: These claims (C1, C18-C45, C50, C55-C57, C62, C69-C70, C82-C87, C93-C94, C98-C105, C111-C113, C123, C128-C141, C176-C200) represent established knowledge from prior research, supported by appropriate citations. They provide necessary context but are not novel findings of this study. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the cited literature.

result: Methodological details and validation of genetic models, including tamoxifen administration protocols, confirmation of gene deletion by qPCR and immunostaining, and RNA-seq analysis of gene expression changes in mutant embryos.
evaluation: Claims C51, C52, C53, C59, C143, C144, and C145 describe experimental methods and validation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1k. These are well-documented and provide necessary validation of the genetic models used in the study.

result: Loss of FOXC2 modestly increased F-actin and pMLC2 area per cell, but the increase was greatly potentiated by oscillatory shear stress.
evaluation: Claim C160 is supported by in vitro experimental data showing that FOXC2 knockdown has modest effects under static conditions but pronounced effects under OSS, consistent with prior work (C113, C191) and the known role of FOXC2 in responding to OSS.
